cheat_sheet.title: Backend Systems, HTTP and Node.js Foundations — Structural Cheat Sheet
cheat_sheet.introduction: This sheet turns Backend Systems, HTTP and Node.js Foundations into visible relationships. It is a reference for planning, tracing, debugging, and explaining—not a list to memorize.
cheat_sheet.why_it_matters: The level contributes directly to a production-style API service. Each concept helps the learner move from an ambiguous task to a contract, a representation, a verified transition, and an explainable result.

mental_model.summary: Represent the work as pipelines, records, relations, and trust boundaries before translating it into implementation details.
reasoning_cycle: Model variables, state, constraints, and relationships

input_questions: What may be absent or malformed?
output_questions: What shape and state are promised?

core_concepts.title: Client-server boundaries
core_concepts.rule: A client requests a capability; a server validates the request, performs controlled work, and returns a documented response.

core_concepts.title: HTTP methods and resource intent
core_concepts.rule: Methods communicate intent: retrieval, creation, replacement, partial change, and deletion have different safety and idempotency properties.

core_concepts.title: URLs, headers, bodies, and status codes
core_concepts.rule: An HTTP message combines routing data, metadata, optional content, and a status that summarizes the outcome.

core_concepts.title: Node.js modules and runtime state
core_concepts.rule: A Node process loads modules into a dependency graph and keeps process-wide state separate from request-specific values.

core_concepts.title: Event loop and asynchronous I/O
core_concepts.rule: The event loop schedules callbacks after I/O completes; CPU-heavy work blocks progress while pending I/O does not.

core_concepts.title: Configuration, files, and environment values
core_concepts.rule: Configuration varies by environment and belongs outside source code; paths and failures must be handled explicitly.

core_concepts.title: Building a minimal request pipeline
core_concepts.rule: A server pipeline parses a request, routes it, performs domain work, and serializes one response exactly once.

core_concepts.title: Errors, logging, and graceful shutdown
core_concepts.rule: Operational errors need structured context, safe client messages, and orderly resource cleanup during shutdown.

common_mistakes: Starting with syntax before defining the input-output contract.
Combining current state and a candidate update so rejection cannot be safe.
Treating an observed normal result as proof for every boundary.
Choosing a structure because it is familiar rather than because its operations match the constraints.
Ignoring empty, missing, duplicate, maximum-size, repeated, or out-of-order cases.
Hiding failures instead of representing loading, empty, rejected, and error states explicitly.
Optimizing before measuring the actual bottleneck or risk.
Explaining what the implementation does without explaining why its invariant proves correctness.
debugging_checklist: Can I restate the exact expected output?
Are input shape, units, identity, and trust level explicit?
Which state is allowed to change?
Which invariant should hold after every step?
What is the first observed step that differs from the expected trace?
Is the boundary inclusive or exclusive?
Can an invalid or repeated event mutate valid state?
Are asynchronous or external results stale, missing, or out of order?
Does the representation match the operation mix and constraints?
Did the repair pass the original failure and nearby regression cases?

lessons.title: Client-server boundaries
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Client-server boundaries within a reliable request-processing service.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Client-server boundaries to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Client-server boundaries is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. A client requests a capability; a server validates the request, performs controlled work, and returns a documented response.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Client-server boundaries, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use pipelines, records, relations, and trust boundaries. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

inputs: The data or event that activates Client-server boundaries
outputs: A value, decision, or visible state matching the contract
A preserved or deliberately updated next state
Evidence explaining acceptance or rejection

variables_and_state.name: candidate_input
variables_and_state.role: The untrusted or unverified incoming value

variables_and_state.name: current_state
variables_and_state.role: The last state known to satisfy all invariants

variables_and_state.name: constraint_result
variables_and_state.role: The explicit validation outcome

variables_and_state.name: next_state
variables_and_state.role: A proposed state computed without corrupting current_state

constraints: Inputs must match the declared shape and permitted boundary.
A rejected input must not corrupt the previous valid state.
The output must be representable by the current application workflow.
Every external or user-provided value is validated before use.
invariants: The governing relationship remains true: A client requests a capability; a server validates the request, performs controlled work, and returns a documented response.
At most one documented commit occurs for one accepted transition.
Invalid input leaves the last valid state unchanged.
step_by_step_reasoning: Restate the problem as a testable input-output contract.
List state variables and separate current state from a candidate update.
Write constraints as predicates with visible boundary choices.
Apply the structural rule for Client-server boundaries.
Trace the normal case one transition at a time.
Trace an exact boundary and one invalid case.
Compare observed output and preserved invariants with the contract.
Record the first divergent state if the check fails.

worked_examples.title: Normal case: contract to verified output
worked_examples.scenario: A learner applies Client-server boundaries while building a reliable request-processing service.
worked_examples.input: One well-formed input that satisfies the documented preconditions.
reasoning: Name the observable output before choosing an operation.
Represent only the state and relationships needed for that output.
A client requests a capability; a server validates the request, performs controlled work, and returns a documented response.
Trace the transition and compare the result with the contract.
worked_examples.output: A valid state transition with the promised result and recorded evidence.

worked_examples.title: Boundary case: valid at the limit
worked_examples.scenario: The input is exactly at the smallest or largest documented valid boundary.
worked_examples.input: A boundary value explicitly included by the constraint.
reasoning: Write the inclusive or exclusive boundary symbolically.
Evaluate the predicate before changing state.
Apply the same rule used for ordinary valid input.
Verify that the output remains representable and accessible.
worked_examples.output: The boundary case is accepted once and produces a valid output without special hidden state.

worked_examples.title: Rejected case: preserve the invariant
worked_examples.scenario: An input violates one required relationship or arrives in an unsupported state.
worked_examples.input: An out-of-contract value paired with a previously valid state.
reasoning: Identify the failed constraint and stop before commit.
Keep the previous valid state unchanged.
Return a specific, non-sensitive explanation or recovery path.
Record the case as evidence for a regression check.
worked_examples.output: A controlled rejection, preserved prior state, and actionable feedback.

structured_representation.caption: A validate-before-commit trace for Client-server boundaries.

common_mistakes: Beginning implementation before defining the required output.
Changing state before the input or transition has been validated.
Memorizing the label 'Client-server boundaries' without applying its governing relationship.
Testing only one convenient normal case and assuming boundaries behave identically.
edge_cases: The smallest valid input or empty valid structure, when allowed.
The largest documented input, count, depth, size, or duration.
A duplicate, repeated event, retry, or already-completed transition.
Malformed, missing, stale, unauthorized, or otherwise out-of-contract input.
debugging_strategy: Freeze the first input that produces a wrong observable result.
Write the expected trace beside the observed trace.
Locate the first row where state, constraint, or output diverges.
Repair the rule or boundary responsible for that first divergence.
Rerun the failing case plus one normal, one boundary, and one rejection case.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: HTTP methods and resource intent is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Methods communicate intent: retrieval, creation, replacement, partial change, and deletion have different safety and idempotency properties.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For HTTP methods and resource intent, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Event loop and asynchronous I/O is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. The event loop schedules callbacks after I/O completes; CPU-heavy work blocks progress while pending I/O does not.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Event loop and asynchronous I/O, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

project.title: Backend Systems, HTTP and Node.js Foundations: Production-Style Api Service
project.real_world_context: A small team needs a reliable request-processing service that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate production-style API service that demonstrates all eight skills from Backend Systems, HTTP and Node.js Foundations. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: A client requests a capability; a server validates the request, performs controlled work, and returns a documented response.
Methods communicate intent: retrieval, creation, replacement, partial change, and deletion have different safety and idempotency properties.
An HTTP message combines routing data, metadata, optional content, and a status that summarizes the outcome.
A Node process loads modules into a dependency graph and keeps process-wide state separate from request-specific values.
The event loop schedules callbacks after I/O completes; CPU-heavy work blocks progress while pending I/O does not.
Configuration varies by environment and belongs outside source code; paths and failures must be handled explicitly.
A server pipeline parses a request, routes it, performs domain work, and serializes one response exactly once.
Operational errors need structured context, safe client messages, and orderly resource cleanup during shutdown.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Express applications and routers is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Routers partition the URL-method space into cohesive resource contracts instead of one growing conditional chain.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Express applications and routers, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

lessons.title: Validation and normalization
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Validation and normalization within a reliable request-processing service.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Validation and normalization to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Validation and normalization is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Validate shape and constraints at the boundary, then normalize accepted data into one internal representation.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Validation and normalization, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax

lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Route tests and contract verification to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Route tests and contract verification is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Route tests control dependencies and assert status, headers, response shape, and side effects at meaningful boundaries.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Route tests and contract verification, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

project.title: Express, Routing, Middleware and Validation: Production-Style Api Service
project.real_world_context: A small team needs a reliable request-processing service that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate production-style API service that demonstrates all eight skills from Express, Routing, Middleware and Validation. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: Routers partition the URL-method space into cohesive resource contracts instead of one growing conditional chain.
Use path values for identity, query values for optional views, and bodies for structured commands or resource data.
Middleware is an ordered pipeline; each stage either terminates the response or passes a well-defined request state forward.
Validate shape and constraints at the boundary, then normalize accepted data into one internal representation.
Domain, validation, and infrastructure failures map to stable error responses without exposing internal secrets.
Resources use stable nouns, consistent representations, and predictable method semantics across collections and members.
Browser trust rules, protective headers, and fair-use limits reduce risk when configured for explicit origins and operations.
Route tests control dependencies and assert status, headers, response shape, and side effects at meaningful boundaries.

constraints: Use only the languages, components, or structural interactions supported by the target application environment.
Do not hide invalid input, unavailable data, or failure behind a successful-looking state.
Keep current valid state recoverable until a candidate transition passes validation.
Do not embed secrets, real credentials, personal data, or private endpoints.
Make all important output and error states accessible and testable.
Record assumptions and unsupported cases explicitly.
The submitted result must be reproducible from the included instructions.

test_cases.expected: one correct output and valid next state

test_cases.condition: second valid input with different data

test_cases.expected: accepted only if contract includes it

test_cases.condition: valid retry after a controlled failure

maximum documented size
duplicate or retry
out-of-order or stale result
malformed or unauthorized input
debugging_checklist: Freeze a reproducible failing input.
Compare expected and observed traces.
Find the first divergent state.
Check the constraint at that transition.
Repair cause before symptoms.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Relations, rows, columns, and keys is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. A relational table represents a set of similarly shaped facts; keys identify rows and connect related sets.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Relations, rows, columns, and keys, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use pipelines, records, relations, and trust boundaries. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

constraints: Inputs must match the declared shape and permitted boundary.
A rejected input must not corrupt the previous valid state.
The output must be representable by the current application workflow.
Every external or user-provided value is validated before use.

At most one documented commit occurs for one accepted transition.
Invalid input leaves the last valid state unchanged.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Selecting, filtering, and ordering is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. A query transforms a relation by choosing columns, retaining rows that satisfy predicates, and applying order only when requested.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Selecting, filtering, and ordering, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Writes, constraints, and transactions is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. A transaction moves the database from one valid state to another atomically while constraints guard invariants.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Writes, constraints, and transactions, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

project.title: Databases, SQL, Data Modeling and Queries: Production-Style Api Service
project.real_world_context: A small team needs a reliable request-processing service that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate production-style API service that demonstrates all eight skills from Databases, SQL, Data Modeling and Queries. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: A relational table represents a set of similarly shaped facts; keys identify rows and connect related sets.
Cardinality states how many records may relate, determining whether a foreign key or junction table represents the relationship.
A query transforms a relation by choosing columns, retaining rows that satisfy predicates, and applying order only when requested.
A join pairs rows according to a predicate; join type determines which unmatched rows remain in the result.
Grouping partitions rows by keys, then aggregate functions reduce each group to summary values.
A transaction moves the database from one valid state to another atomically while constraints guard invariants.
An index trades write cost and storage for faster ordered lookup; the query plan reveals whether that trade is being used.
Normalization reduces contradictory facts, while versioned migrations change schema and data in controlled, reversible steps.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Password storage and verification is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Store salted slow password hashes, compare them safely, and never retain or log the original secret.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Password storage and verification, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

lessons.title: Cookies, CSRF, and browser sessions
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Cookies, CSRF, and browser sessions within a reliable request-processing service.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Cookies, CSRF, and browser sessions to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Cookies, CSRF, and browser sessions is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Secure cookie attributes protect transport and script access, while CSRF defenses ensure a state-changing request reflects user intent.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Cookies, CSRF, and browser sessions, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use pipelines, records, relations, and trust boundaries. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

outputs: A value, decision, or visible state matching the contract

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Threat modeling and layered controls is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Threat modeling and layered controls, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate production-style API service that demonstrates all eight skills from Authentication, Authorization and Application Security. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

core_concepts.title: Queues and background jobs

core_concepts.rule: Concurrent requests can interleave; atomic constraints and idempotency keys protect shared-state invariants.

core_concepts.title: Containers, deployment, and health checks

common_mistakes: Starting with syntax before defining the input-output contract.
Combining current state and a candidate update so rejection cannot be safe.
Treating an observed normal result as proof for every boundary.
Choosing a structure because it is familiar rather than because its operations match the constraints.
Ignoring empty, missing, duplicate, maximum-size, repeated, or out-of-order cases.
Hiding failures instead of representing loading, empty, rejected, and error states explicitly.
Optimizing before measuring the actual bottleneck or risk.
Explaining what the implementation does without explaining why its invariant proves correctness.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Versioning, pagination, and compatibility is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

lessons.title: Observability with logs, metrics, and traces
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Observability with logs, metrics, and traces within a reliable request-processing service.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Observability with logs, metrics, and traces to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Observability with logs, metrics, and traces is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Logs explain events, metrics reveal aggregate behavior, and traces connect work across a distributed request path.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Observability with logs, metrics, and traces, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use pipelines, records, relations, and trust boundaries. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

inputs: The data or event that activates Observability with logs, metrics, and traces

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Concurrency and idempotent operations is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Concurrent requests can interleave; atomic constraints and idempotency keys protect shared-state invariants.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Concurrency and idempotent operations, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

project.title: Production APIs, Testing, Deployment and Scaling: Production-Style Api Service
project.real_world_context: A small team needs a reliable request-processing service that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate production-style API service that demonstrates all eight skills from Production APIs, Testing, Deployment and Scaling. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: Evolve contracts deliberately; pagination bounds work, and compatibility rules prevent existing clients from breaking unexpectedly.
Use many fast unit tests, focused integration tests, and a small number of end-to-end tests around the highest-risk journeys.
Logs explain events, metrics reveal aggregate behavior, and traces connect work across a distributed request path.
A cache is a derived copy with a freshness policy; keys, lifetime, invalidation, and failure behavior determine correctness.
A queue separates arrival from processing; acknowledgments, retries, dead-letter handling, and idempotency prevent silent loss or duplicate harm.
Concurrent requests can interleave; atomic constraints and idempotency keys protect shared-state invariants.
A deployable service has reproducible artifacts, explicit configuration, health signals, migrations, and safe rollout/rollback steps.
Capacity planning connects arrival rate, service time, utilization, latency, redundancy, and recovery objectives.

starter_materials.scaffold_policy: Level 5 supplies only constraints, acceptance criteria, and review checkpoints.

mandatory_features: Demonstrate Versioning, pagination, and compatibility and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Testing pyramid and controlled dependencies and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Observability with logs, metrics, and traces and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Caching and invalidation and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Queues and background jobs and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Concurrency and idempotent operations and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Containers, deployment, and health checks and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Scaling, reliability, and capacity and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
constraints: Use only the languages, components, or structural interactions supported by the target application environment.
Do not hide invalid input, unavailable data, or failure behind a successful-looking state.
Keep current valid state recoverable until a candidate transition passes validation.
Do not embed secrets, real credentials, personal data, or private endpoints.
Make all important output and error states accessible and testable.
Record assumptions and unsupported cases explicitly.
The submitted result must be reproducible from the included instructions.

test_cases.expected: one correct output and valid next state

test_cases.condition: second valid input with different data

test_cases.expected: accepted only if contract includes it

test_cases.condition: valid retry after a controlled failure

edge_cases: empty or minimum
maximum documented size
duplicate or retry
out-of-order or stale result
malformed or unauthorized input
debugging_checklist: Freeze a reproducible failing input.
Compare expected and observed traces.
Find the first divergent state.
Check the constraint at that transition.
Repair cause before symptoms.
Rerun the failure and adjacent cases.
Confirm state recovery and accessible feedback.
Record the limitation if the case remains unsupported.
completion_checklist: All eight level skills appear in the artifact or evidence.
The input-output contract is complete.
The structural model matches the implementation or decision flow.
All eight required test categories have evidence.
The rubric self-score totals 100 possible points.
No secret, real credential, or sensitive personal data is included.
Submission instructions reproduce the result.
Reflection names one failure, repair, and justified improvement.
submission_requirements: README with setup or review instructions

rubric.evidence: inputs, outputs, constraints, diagram, and milestones
mandatory behavior matches the project contract
clear responsibilities, transitions, and dependency boundaries
normal, boundary, invalid, repeated, and failure cases
usable states, safe handling, and recovery feedback
setup, decisions, limitations, evidence, and reproducible instructions
first divergence, repair, trade-off, and next iteration

common_failure_conditions: The result handles only one normal case.
State changes before validation.
A level skill is named but not demonstrated.
The diagram disagrees with the implemented flow.
A failed dependency leaves a false success state.
Submission evidence cannot be reproduced.
reflection_questions: Which assumption changed after the first trace?
Where did expected and observed state first diverge?
Which invariant prevented the most serious failure?
What trade-off did you make among clarity, cost, performance, accessibility, safety, or flexibility?
What evidence would you collect before a wider release?
optional_extensions: Add a second representation and compare which relationships become easier to inspect.
Add property-based or generated boundary cases without duplicating existing tests.
Measure one performance, quality, or risk indicator and justify an improvement threshold.
Design a migration or compatibility plan for one changed requirement.
project.acceptable_outcome_example: A submission may use the supplied contract and state templates, implement one complete primary journey, show all required failure states, and provide eight passing test records plus one documented limitation. The exact implementation remains the learner's work.

prompts.prompt: Restate the final input-output contract in one sentence.
Describe the first state where expected and observed behavior diverged.
Explain the repair and the invariant or constraint it restored.
Name one design trade-off and the evidence behind your choice.
What is the safest and most valuable next improvement?
